---
title: "Branching and Writing"
---

Pinning makes the past reproducible. *Branching* makes the present safe to
change: `tether new` sets up a fresh writable branch in every system off the
pinned state, you write through native handles, and `commit` pins the results.
Nothing you do on your branches touches `main` in any system until you decide
it should.

This walkthrough continues from [Pinning](03-pinning.qmd) and adds a Lance
feature store and the analysis code itself as objects, so the recipe covers
four different systems.

## Register a few more objects

```bash
tether add features --kind lance s3://bucket/features.lance
tether add code     --kind git ../analysis-code --remote origin
tether commit -m "Add feature store and code"
```

`code` pins a *separate* git repository -- the analysis code -- at its `HEAD`
sha (as a tag), so a dataset commit also names the code that produced it. Do
not register the repository the dataset itself lives in: every `tether commit`
moves its sha, so every `pull` would find it behind and re-pin it forever.

## Fork: `tether new`

```bash
tether new main
```

```
working refs set up
  code          -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.code          (created on first writable open)
  db/metrics    -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.db-metrics    (created on first writable open)
  features      -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.features      (created on first writable open)
  zarr/imaging  -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.zarr-imaging  (created on first writable open)
```

For every Forkable object, `new` decided a branch name and where it will be
forked from -- and wrote nothing. Forking is **lazy** by default: the branch is
created by the first writable `open` of that object, from the pin recorded at
`main`. A workspace that reads three objects and writes one ends up with one
branch, not four.

| Object | Pin at `main` | Working ref (created on first write) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `zarr/imaging` | Icechunk tag | Icechunk branch `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.zarr-imaging` |
| `db/metrics` | Neon branch | Neon child branch `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.db-metrics` |
| `features` | Lance tag | Lance branch `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.features` |
| `code` | git tag | git branch `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.code` |

`0a1b2c3d` is the dataset's id (from `tether.toml`) and `7c1e0a4d` this
workspace's (from the untracked `.tether/workspace.toml`), so two people -- or
two jj workspaces, or two datasets sharing a store -- forking the same commit
get disjoint branches everywhere. `raw/plate1` has no working ref: files
cannot be forked.

`status` reads objects that have not been forked yet at their base (the pin),
and all are `clean`; once a branch exists, `status` reads it instead.

### Lazy or eager

`tether new --eager` (or `[new] fork = "eager"` in `tether.toml`) creates every
branch during `new`, which is how tether worked before 0.1.0a6. Every fork in
every backend is a copy-on-write pointer, so the difference is not the cost of
creating a branch; it is what an idle branch *holds* and *needs*:

| | Lazy (default) | Eager |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branches created | only for objects you actually write | one per Forkable object, every `new` |
| What a forgotten workspace leaves behind | nothing for untouched objects | a branch per object -- each a GC root that keeps its snapshot alive and a line in every branch list; Neon counts them against the project's branch quota |
| Credentials needed at `new` | read only | write, for every system |
| First writable `open` | pays the fork (one metadata write, plus a cheap pin check) | just opens |
| `--dry-run` | `new --dry-run` shows `defer-fork`; the fork itself happens inside `open`, which has no dry run -- use `new --eager --dry-run` to preview what would be created | `new --dry-run` shows every `fork` |
| HEAD moves before you write | the workspace is stale; `new` re-decides with nothing to reset | `new` resets the branches |
| The pin is deleted before you write (`gc` on another machine) | `open` fails with `pin missing` -- the fork never happened | the branch already exists and keeps the data |
| Pre-creating branches for a job | `Repo.materialize_fork(key)` per object, or `--eager` | automatic |

If one system refuses to fork (quota, network), `new` still records the
branches it did create and names the object that failed; run `new` again once
the cause is gone -- existing branches are reset onto the pin, never
duplicated.

The last two rows are the same trade-off: a pin is durable, so deferring the
fork is safe as long as the pin outlives the wait -- which it does unless
someone drops the commit that references it and runs `gc` in between.

**Pin-less objects are never deferred.** With `--pin record` there is no tag;
the recorded state is a bare snapshot id / version / commit / LSN that the
system will eventually expire (Icechunk `expire_snapshots`, Iceberg snapshot
expiry, Lance `cleanup_old_versions`, Neon's history window). A branch on it is
the only thing that stops that. So `new` forks those immediately even in lazy
mode -- the plan says `fork ... forked now so the state cannot expire` -- and
the trade-off above does not apply to them.

## Write through native handles

`open` without `-r` returns a **writable** handle for Forkable objects,
positioned on the working ref. tether hands you the system's own objects and
gets out of the way.

### Icechunk

```python
import zarr
from tether import Repo
from tether.handles import IcechunkHandle

repo = Repo.find(".")
h = repo.open("zarr/imaging")
assert isinstance(h, IcechunkHandle) and not h.read_only
print(h.branch)                       # tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.zarr-imaging

group = zarr.open_group(h.session.store, mode="a")
group["labels"][...] = relabel(group["labels"][...])
h.session.commit("Relabel plate1 with model v3")   # an Icechunk commit on the fork
```

### Lance

```python
import lance, pyarrow as pa
from tether.handles import LanceHandle

h = repo.open("features")
assert isinstance(h, LanceHandle)
lance.write_dataset(pa.table({"well": ["A1"], "score": [0.91]}), h.dataset, mode="append")
```

### Neon (any Postgres client)

```python
import psycopg
from tether.handles import NeonHandle

h = repo.open("db/metrics")
assert isinstance(h, NeonHandle)
with psycopg.connect(h.url) as conn:     # URL for the forked branch's endpoint
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO metrics (well, score) VALUES ('A1', 0.91)")
```

Opening a Neon fork writable creates a `read_write` compute endpoint on the
branch if none exists; the URL points at it.

::: {.callout-note title="Neon: pins are children of the branch they were taken on"}
A Neon pin is a branch at an LSN, and a pin taken on your working branch is a
*child* of it. That shapes what `new` and `gc` can do afterwards:

- `commit` then `new` keeps your working branch: it already sits at the state
  that was just pinned from it, so the plan says `reuse` and nothing is reset.
- `new` onto a *different* pin (an older commit, a teammate's) cannot reset a
  branch that has pin children -- Neon will not restore it in place -- so the
  fork lands on a sibling name (`...db-61a22c.2`) and the old branch stays as
  the pins' parent. Your workspace records the sibling.
- Neither `gc --prune-workspaces` nor `--force-prune` can delete a branch
  while pins hang off it; the plan lists it as `keep-branch: cannot be
  deleted` with the pins named. Release those pins first (drop the commits
  that reference them, `gc`), then the branch goes.

Icechunk, Iceberg, Lance, lakeFS, and Dolt pins are tags or independent refs,
so none of this applies to them.
:::

### Code

```python
from tether.handles import GitHandle

h = repo.open("code")
assert isinstance(h, GitHandle)
h.sha, h.path        # the fork branch's head; commit your code changes there
```

From the shell, `tether open <key>` prints the same addresses:

```bash
tether open db/metrics
postgresql://runner@ep-brisk-forest-x9y8z7.us-west-2.aws.neon.tech/metrics?...
tether open features
s3://bucket/features.lance#tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.features@v4
```

## See what changed

```bash
tether status --snapshot
```

```
dataset 3ba1c07e55d2
  modified  code  [git/forkable]
  modified  db/metrics  [neon/forkable]
  modified  features  [lance/forkable]
     clean  raw/plate1  [file/observed] unrecoverable
  modified  zarr/imaging  [icechunk/forkable]
```

`diff` with no arguments compares the current commit's manifests with the
working tree; nothing has been recorded yet, so use `--content` after the
commit below. Meanwhile `main` in every system is untouched: the forks isolate
your work.

## Commit: pin the forks

```bash
tether commit -m "Relabel plate1 with model v3; scores for A1"
```

```
  pinned code -> tether.0a1b2c3d.f01a9d3c2b7ee5f6
  pinned db/metrics -> tether.0a1b2c3d.55e2ab7d9c10e5f6
  pinned features -> tether.0a1b2c3d.9e7c4b2f0a61e5f6
  pinned zarr/imaging -> tether.0a1b2c3d.deb4861eb388e5f6
committed 41c0d9e2b7f3
```

Each pin points at the state of the *working branch*: an Icechunk tag on the
fork's snapshot, a Lance tag on `(branch, version)`, a Neon branch at the
fork's LSN, a git tag on the fork's sha. Then the manifests were committed.
Now compare:

```bash
tether diff main @- --content
```

```
    changed  code  [+0 -0 ~1 files]
               modified  segment.py  +12 -3
    changed  db/metrics
    changed  features  [+1 -0 ~0 fragments]
                  added  fragment 4  +1 rows
    changed  zarr/imaging  [+0 -0 ~1 nodes]
               modified  /labels  12 chunks
```

Continue writing on the same forks and committing as often as you like; each
commit pins the latest state and the previous pins stay valid (they are what
`open -r` and `verify` use).

## Bringing it back to `main`: `tether promote`

Your dataset commit pins the fork's state in every system. To make each
system's *base branch* point at that state too -- jj's `squash --into main`,
for data -- run:

```bash
tether promote --dry-run
```

```
plan: promote (3 write(s))
        fast-forward  code          [git] main  main sha=41c0d9e2b7f3… -> sha=f01a9d3c2b7e… (base unchanged since fork)
        fast-forward  features      [lance] main  ...
        fast-forward  zarr/imaging  [icechunk] main  main snapshot_id=K3F9M2A1B7C8… -> snapshot_id=DEB4861EB388… (base unchanged since fork)
              refuse  db/metrics    [neon] main  the neon backend cannot move a branch; Neon cannot promote a child branch into its parent; use `--write direct` ...
```

For each Forkable object tether compares the base branch to the **fork point**
-- the state recorded in `workspace.toml` when the branch was created -- and
decides:

| Base branch since your fork | Backend has | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| unchanged | `PROMOTE` | **fast-forward**: the base is moved to the fork's head; nothing is rewritten |
| moved | `MERGE` | **merge**: the system's own three-way merge (lakeFS `merge_into`, Dolt `DOLT_MERGE`, `git merge`); conflicts are reported and nothing is written |
| moved | `PROMOTE` only | **refuse**, with the system's recipe (Icechunk and Iceberg have no merge) |
| anything | neither | **refuse** (Neon, Lance) |

`--strategy ff` refuses anything that is not a fast-forward -- the setting for
CI, where a surprise merge is worse than a failure. `--strategy merge` refuses
plain fast-forwards when you want a merge commit for the record. `--rev REV`
promotes what a *dataset commit* pinned instead of this workspace's live
branches (the ancestry check replaces the fork point). `--dry-run`, `--plan`,
and `--from-plan` work as everywhere else; apply refuses if a base moved after
the plan was made.

After a **fast-forward** nothing tether-side changes: the manifests already
named that state and the pin already held it. Land the dataset commit with
`jj` and you are done. After a **merge** the base holds a state no commit has
pinned yet, so `promote` resets your working branch onto the merge result and
the next `tether commit` pins it -- the output says so.

```bash
tether promote                      # fast-forward what it can, merge where the system can
tether commit -m "Merge plate1 relabel into main"   # only after a merge
jj bookmark set main -r @-          # land the dataset commit
```

Refusals are the honest part. Icechunk and Iceberg can fast-forward but not
merge; if `main` moved under you, re-apply the writes on a fresh fork (or, for
Icechunk, `reset_branch` when discarding `main`'s newer snapshots is what you
mean). Lance cannot move a branch head at all yet. Neon cannot promote a child
branch into its parent -- use `--write direct` for databases that must receive
writes, so the working ref *is* `main` and pins (child branches at an LSN)
provide reproducibility.

## Positions: what the next commit records

A dataset commit records an exact state per object. Between commits each
object has a *position* -- what the next commit will record -- and it works
the way files do in a VCS: what you did not touch stays exactly as the last
commit had it.

- An object with a **working branch** (forked by `new`, or the base branch
  itself for `write = "direct"`) is positioned at that branch's head. `commit`
  fingerprints it; writes move it.
- An object **without** one keeps its **previous pin** (or recorded state).
  `commit` does not contact its store -- there is nothing it could learn: the
  pin cannot move. If the upstream branch (`locator.branch`) has moved on, or
  the table has a newer version, or the files changed, that is the world's
  business until you *pull*; `status --snapshot` reports it as `behind`.
- An object with **no commit yet** is read once, at the branch head or at
  `--at`.

Systems without branches (files, Iceberg, Delta, DuckLake) follow the same
rule: `pull` reads the current version or the path. The one exception is a
`file = "immutable"` object that changed -- `pull` refuses it like
`status --snapshot` does, since accepting a new state is a re-registration,
not a pull.

`tether pull` is the explicit step that moves positions to upstream -- the
dataset's `git fetch` + rebase:

```bash
tether pull                     # every object without a working branch
tether pull zarr/imaging        # just this one
```

```
  pulled zarr/imaging  snapshot_id=TYZ25DJEHXER -> snapshot_id=AZ1REKMV3HET  (pending working branch will fork from here, not the pin)
  up to date db/metrics
  skipped features: has working branch tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.features-9b2e4f; commit it, or `new --discard`
commit to pin the pulled states; `tether undo` puts them back
```

The pulled state is held in the workspace (`status` shows `pulled`) until the
next `commit` pins it; a writable `open` before then forks from it, so "pull,
then work on top" is a rebase onto upstream. `pull` writes nothing to any
store; `undo` reverses it. An object whose working branch *exists* is skipped
-- replacing the branch would discard its writes; commit them, or `new
--discard`.

For a dataset that should trail `main` on every commit, pass `commit --pull`
or set `[commit] pull = true`; the plan then says `pulled from main`.

### Starting from an older snapshot

`--at` sets an object's *initial* position: a state that was never pinned --
an older Icechunk snapshot from before you adopted tether, a Lance version, a
Dolt or lakeFS commit. `tether log` shows what there is to choose from, with
each system's own ids, timestamps, and messages, and marks branches, tags,
and tether pins:

```bash
tether log zarr/imaging                         # a registered object
tether log s3://bucket/imaging.icechunk --kind icechunk   # before registering
```

```
  AZ1REKMV3HETD2X7EW7G  2026-09-05 15:16  Relabel plate1 with model v3  [main]
  TYZ25DJEHXERGBR7H3P0  2026-09-05 14:02  Segment plate1
  M32R7C6M4H4Y8BEGSEK0  2026-09-05 13:40  Convert plate1
  1CECHNKREP0F1RSTCMT0  2026-09-05 13:39  Repository initialized
```

```bash
tether add zarr/imaging --kind icechunk s3://bucket/imaging.icechunk --at TYZ25DJEHXERGBR7H3P0
tether commit -m "Adopt imaging at the pre-relabel snapshot"
tether new
```

`--pick` does the same interactively -- it prints the list numbered and asks
which entry to use:

```bash
tether add zarr/imaging --kind icechunk s3://bucket/imaging.icechunk --pick
```

```
  1. AZ1REKMV3HETD2X7EW7G  2026-09-05 15:16  Relabel plate1 with model v3  [main]
  2. TYZ25DJEHXERGBR7H3P0  2026-09-05 14:02  Segment plate1
  3. M32R7C6M4H4Y8BEGSEK0  2026-09-05 13:40  Convert plate1
  4. 1CECHNKREP0F1RSTCMT0  2026-09-05 13:39  Repository initialized
Pick an entry (number or id) [1]: 2
added zarr/imaging (icechunk) at TYZ25DJEHXERGBR7H3P0
```

The first `commit` pins that state, `open` reads it, and `new` forks from the
pin, exactly as if it had been the branch head. After that `at` has no further
role: the pin is the position, and `tether pull` moves the object onto `main`
(dropping `at` from the manifest). The ids `tether log` prints are always
valid `at` values; the per-system forms are in the
[backends guide](09-backends.qmd). Neon and files have no `at`.

## `direct` mode: write on the base branch

Some objects should never be forked -- a production database, a shared
`main` you deliberately advance. Register them with `--write direct`:

```bash
tether add db/prod --kind neon --project-id prj-9f2 --database prod --role app --write direct
```

For a `direct` object, `tether new` sets the working ref to the locator's branch
(`main`) instead of forking. `open` still returns a writable handle -- to
`main` -- and `commit` still pins whatever state it finds there. You get
reproducibility without branch sprawl, and the Neon quiescence check
(`commit` refuses while writers are active unless `--force`) keeps pins
consistent.

## Stale working copies

If an object's committed manifest changes under you -- a teammate committed
it, or you `jj new` to another revision where it is pinned differently -- your
fork of it was taken from a state that is no longer the dataset's:

```bash
tether status
```

```
dataset 9d0e5f71ac22 (STALE: zarr/imaging)
  ...
```

```bash
tether open zarr/imaging
error: working copy is stale: the committed state of zarr/imaging changed since this workspace forked; run `tether new` to refork before writing
```

Staleness is per object: the other forks stay writable, your own commits never
make you stale, and adding or removing unrelated objects does not clear it.

`tether new` re-decides from the current pins and clears the flag. Everything
you *committed* is safe: those pins are tags, independent of any branch. Writes
you did not commit are not: re-forking an existing branch resets it to the new
pin (Icechunk `reset_branch`, Lance/lakeFS/Dolt delete-and-recreate, git
`branch -f`, Neon branch restore). `new` therefore looks at every branch it
would reset first, and refuses if one holds writes beyond what you last
committed:

```
$ tether new
error: refusing to reset working branches with unpinned writes:
  zarr/imaging: tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.zarr-imaging-3fa1c0 has writes since this workspace last committed (snapshot_id=Q7ZK…); commit them, or pass --discard to throw them away
```

Commit, or `tether new --discard` if that was scratch work. Branches that
were still pending are simply re-decided; there was nothing to reset.

## Undo

Every command that touched a store is in this workspace's operation log:

```bash
tether ops
```

```
9f2e1c7b3a5d  2026-09-05T10:41:12+00:00  commit   pinned zarr/imaging, db/metrics; vcs 4c1e2a9b7d3f
3f1c9a2b7d4e  2026-09-05T10:22:03+00:00  fork     forked zarr/imaging -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.7c1e0a4d.zarr-imaging-3fa1c0
b7d4e3f1c9a2  2026-09-05T10:21:55+00:00  new      deferred code, db/metrics, features, zarr/imaging; at main
```

`tether undo` reverses the newest entry where the store still allows it. Undo
the commit and it is *uncommitted*: the dataset commit leaves the VCS, the
manifests are working-tree changes again, and the pins stay -- they are still
referenced, so `gc` keeps them and `tether commit` re-records them. Undo the
fork and the branch is deleted (refused, like `new`, if it gained writes you
never committed -- `--discard` overrides) and `workspace.toml` goes back to
saying the fork is pending. Undo the `new` and the working copy returns to
where it was, too.

```bash
tether undo            # the commit -> uncommitted; pins kept
tether undo            # the fork  -> branch deleted, fork pending again
tether ops             # both entries now read "(undone by ...)"
```

What undo cannot do it says so: a `gc` that deleted pins gets its branches
and listings back but reports the pins as `IRREVERSIBLE` (exit code 2); a
`promote` is refused with the previous base heads printed. `jj undo` and
`git reset` stay what they were -- they move the manifests, never the stores;
tether's undo is the other half.

If a store lost something a manifest promises -- a pin deleted by hand, a
branch this workspace expects -- `tether repair` recreates it from the recorded
state, while the store still has that state.

## Workspaces

Because working refs live in the *untracked* `.tether/workspace.toml`, each
jj workspace (or each checkout) is an independent tether workspace with its own
id and its own forks. Two agents working on the same dataset commit never write
to the same branch.

## Recap

- `tether new [rev]` decides a writable branch per Forkable object off the pins
  at `rev`; names embed the workspace id so forks never collide. By default the
  branch is created on the first writable `open` (`--eager` creates them all
  now; `--pin record` objects always fork now).
- `open` returns writable native handles on those forks; write with the
  system's own library.
- `promote` moves each system's base branch to the fork: fast-forward when the
  base is unchanged since the fork point, native merge where the system has
  one, refusal with the system's recipe otherwise.
- `commit` pins the forks' states and commits the manifests; `diff --content`
  shows what changed inside each system.
- Promotion to `main` is per system and deliberate; `--write direct` skips
  forking for objects that must stay on their base branch.
